Arjuna
(‘the white or the pure’)
------------------------------------------
The most widely known of the five Pāṇḍava princes, the great hero of the कुरुक्षेत्र war and the instrumental cause of the immortal Bhagavadgītā, अर्जुन occupies a very important place in the epic Mahābhārata. Born to कुन्ती, the senior queen of the king पाण्डु, by the grace of the god इन्द्र, अर्जुन exhibited his valour and skill in archery even from his childhood days, thus becoming the most favourite disciple of द्रोणाचार्य, the superb master of the science of archery. Bent upon settling scores with the king Drupada, who had humiliated him, द्रोणाचार्य sought अर्जुन’s help in humbling the king’s pride. अर्जुन responded enthusiastically and fulfilled his गुरु’s wish. Later, disguised as a ब्राह्मण, अर्जुन successfully pierced the matsya-यन्त्र (a contrivance for testing the skill in archery) and won the hand of द्रौपदी, Drupada’s daughter. However, a curious interference of fate made द्रौपदी, the common wife of all the Pāṇḍava princes. Apart from द्रौपदी, अर्जुन had three more wives: सुभद्रा, Ulūpī and चित्राङ्गदा.
Once he performed severe penance at the Indrakīla mountains to propitiate Lord शिव. शिव however appeared in the guise of a hunter chieftain and man-oeuvred a situation in which अर्जुन was obliged to fight him! Of course शिव was pleased with his courage and prowess, and granted him the celestial weapon pāśupatāstra.
Living in disguise under the assumed name बृहन्नला at the court of the king विराट, he taught dancing to विराट’s daughter, उत्तरा. Later he participated in the operation to rescue विराट’s cows from the clutches of the Kauravas, who were decisively beaten in the battle.
Before the कुरुक्षेत्र war, he approached Śrī कृष्ण for help and preferred him (as his charioteer) to the Yādava army without कृष्ण.
At the commencement of the war, he was overcome by intense remorse and abhorrence of the killing involved, and refused to fight. After Śrī कृष्ण’s teaching (known as the Bhagavadgītā) dispelled his इग्नोरन्चे and delusion, he got up and fought, bringing ultimate victory and glory to the Pāṇḍavas.
After कृष्ण’s demise, he went to द्वारका and while escorting the Yādava ladies to Hastināvatī, was ambushed and conquered by robbers, thereby obliging him to realize that all his strength had been derived from कृष्ण’s grace! He died during the महाप्रस्थान (great journey), while ascending to हेअवेन्.
Among his children, अभिमन्यु, the son of सुभद्रा, was slain in the कुरु-क्षेत्र war. बभ्रुवाहन, the son of चित्राङ्गदा became the ruler of Maṇipura. परीक्षित्, the son of अभिमन्यु, succeeded to the royal throne after its abdication by युधिष्ठिर.
Kārtavīrya, the king of हैहय, who was reputed to have one thousand arms, was also known as अर्जुन. (See KĀRTAVĪRYĀRJUNA.)
The well-known Buddhist work Lalitavistara mentions one mathematician अर्जुन who was aware of the system of calculating numerals in multiples of 100, commencing from koṭi (one crore), up to 1053.

—1606)
------------------------------------------
Whether सिखिस्म् is a separate reli-gion or a reform movement in हिन्दुइस्म्, there is no gainsaying the fact that the Sikh Gurus saved हिन्दुइस्म् from external as well as internal dangers and exercised a tremendous influence on the contemporary Hindu society.
Sikhism, founded by गुरु Nānak (A.

—1538) and nurtured by a succession of nine more Gurus, had to pass through various critical periods in its chequered history. गुरु Arjan, the fifth in the line of succession, appeared on the scene just when a serious crisis, which would threaten its very existence, was developing.
He was born at Goindwal in A.

. He was the youngest son of Bhāi Jeṭha (later ordained as गुरु Rām Dās) and Bībi Bhani (daughter of the third गुरु Amar Dās). गुरु Amar Dās is said to have remarked that this child would cruise people across the ocean of life.
Guru Rām Dās, in course of time, appointed Arjan as his successor. After his passing away, when Arjan took over as the next गुरु, Prīti Cand, his eldest brother, who had not reconciled himself to this supersession, started harassing him to the maximum possible extent. However, being too humble and noble to counter him, गुरु Arjan left Goindwal and settled down in a new township. Here he kept himself busy completing the holy tanks of Santokhsar and Amritsar and other works left unfinished by गुरु Rām Dās. It was he who got the foundation stone of Harmandir (later known as the गोल्देन् तेम्प्ले) laid by Mian Mīr, a Muslim saint from Lahore. After the construction of the temple and the lake was over, he undertook an extensive tour of Punjab to meet his disciples and consolidate the work.
Guru Arjan, who had no children till then, sent his wife to Bhāi बुद्ध, a highly respected Sikh saint, to get his blessings. Bhāi बुद्ध blessed her and foretold that the son she would give birth to, would crush the enemies of सिखिस्म् like crushing an onion. She gave birth to Hargobind, (in A.

), who later on succeeded गुरु Arjan.
Prīti Chand’s machinations to usurp power continued. He organized several attempts to kill the child Hargobind who escaped miraculously. However, when he tried to bring out his own compositions, passing them on to the Sikhs as the compositions of नानक्, गुरु Arjan had to act quickly and decisively. He personally went to all the important places connected with the previous Gurus and collected the authentic texts of their Bāṇi (word). This collection subsequently came to be known as the Holy Granth.
Chandu Shāh, a Hindu banker of Delhi who wielded a lot of influence with the Mughal Emperors, was looking for a suitable match for his daughter. When his agents suggested that he marry her to Hargobind, Chandu Shāh pooh-poohed it deriding the Sikh गुरु for lack of social or political status. Later on, when he could not get anyone else, and relented, गुरु Arjan politely declined the offer. This antagonized the influential banker who succeeded in creating troubles for the गुरु at the hands of the Mughal authorities.
Though Akbar himself was well-disposed towards the गुरु, Jehāṅgīr, his successor was not. He levied a heavy fine on the गुरु who however refused to pay it. This incurred the wrath of the emperor who tortured him in various ways. The गुरु however, bore everything with great fortitude. Later (in A.

) he entered the river Ravi and was carried away by its swirling waters.
Guru Arjan has left a large number of hymns (2218) rich in imagery and lending themselves easily to मुसिच्. Sukhmaṇi, his magnum opus ranks only next to the Japji of गुरु Nānak.
